Target User Group

Who are we designing for?

Older adults (65+) with basic digital skills who are now being pushed to bank, book and claim services online

Arthur (72) - Persona Example

Retired clerk who wants to handle his own banking and messages

Scenario & Context

On a fine Monday morning after breakfast, Arthur gets an email on his phone while reading the news with a lucrative business offer. As a clerk, he was always interested in finance so this caught his eye.

He doesn't want to alarm his children who are already worried about his finances. The offer uses complex wording with lots of numbers and text blocks in small format.

He wants to ask a friend, but brushes it off after being a victim of a previous scam. Arthur spends a long time pondering how to validate the legitimacy of the email.

Eventually, he gives up and closes the tab in panic and frustration, ruining his morning.

Forced Online

In-person counters at banks, health services, and pension offices are closing, so going offline isn't an option.

Alone with the Decision

Embarrassment stops people like Arthur from asking family or friends for guidance or help.

Fear Leads to Avoidance

When people can't reliably tell what's safe, they stop using vital online services altogether.

link to SDG 10

Target 10.2: Inclusion for all ages

Promote the social and economic inclusion of all, irrespective of age.

Target 10.3: Equal outcomes

Reduce inequalities of outcome. Everyone has the same access on paper, but older adults can’t safely benefit from it.

PROJECT QUESTION

“How might we design an interactive system or service that promotes digital well-being and inclusivity for older adults with basic digital skills, so they can use online services confidently without the fear of scams?”

Problem Statement

“There are elderly members of our communities and those around the world that feel left guessing as to if an online communication can be trusted.”

Forced into using online tools

Digital migration has accelerated rapidly, requiring individuals of all technological skill levels to perform essential daily operations on digital devices.

Many elderly individuals are coerced into unfamiliar digital channels without sufficient onboarding, guidance, or verification mechanisms to ensure safety.

Closing of in-person communication points

Physical branches and face-to-face services handling sensitive information are shutting down:

  • Banks
  • Health care
  • Government Funding (pension, grants, etc.)

Requirements

GOAL

Check for malicious content and suggest course of action

PRIVACY

Check emails on the device without uploading them and hide personal details

TRANSPARENCY

Explain why something looks safe or unsafe

USABILITY

Voice Control options

USER AGENCY

Let the user make the final decision

ACCESSIBILITY

Be quick to set up (under 10 minutes for a first-time user)

Crazy 8 Concepts

Selected Direction

Call a Friend, Content Classification App & Clippy Assistant

Call A Friend

CONCEPT WORKSHEET & SKETCH

CORE CONCEPT

Slow down and call someone trusted.

INCLUSIVE AND NATURAL

Allows elderly people to feel more comfortable using the internet and reassured through a normal conversation

MAIN RISK

Fear of embarrassment

Content Classification App

CONCEPT WORKSHEET & SKETCH

CORE CONCEPT

App that checks whether content is malicious or not

SAFETY

Alerts the user to potential scams, to prevent them from making crucial mistake, allowing them to feel safer to browser the internet

MAIN RISK

App reporting a false Negative

C@T Assistant

CONCEPT WORKSHEET & SKETCH

CORE CONCEPT

Virtual assistant that chats and guides you when unsure

PRIVACY

Replacing embarrassment of calling a friend while still keeping the natural back and forward flow of a conversation

MAIN RISK

Too indecisive / confident

OUR CHOSEN IDEA

Integrated content classification and more private

Prototype: Concept

Wizard of Oz testing with a paper cat

WHAT WE BUILT

A cardboard cat on a lollipop stick. One teammate played Arthur while another voiced the cat, standing in for the software.

WHAT WE TESTED

Would Arthur ask a friendly cat for help when he felt too embarrassed to call a friend? He talked a suspicious email through with it, out loud.

WHAT WE LEARNED

Talking felt more natural than highlighting text, and the back-and-forth calmed Arthur. The conversation became C@T’s core; the voice became the read-aloud option.

Prototype: Low Fidelity

Mapping the conversation before drawing any screens

THE BACKBONE

We mapped C@T’s whole conversation as a yes/no tree before drawing any screens. Every branch ends in a verdict and a next step.

THE CAT

ChatGPT generated four cat moods: awake, alert, thinking and asleep. Its face shows what C@T is doing at a glance.

Images generated with AI.

WHY LOW FIDELITY

Changing a question or adding a branch took minutes, with no screens to redraw. The tree became the core of the final app: one question per screen.

HOW WE TESTED IT

  • Other lab groups tried it unaided.
  • Team DuckTors ran a heuristic evaluation.
  • A classmate played Arthur in a think-aloud session.
  • The TAs gave feedback.

FEEDBACK & ITERATIONS

WHAT WE FOUNDSEVERITY (1–3)WHAT WE CHANGED
Clicked the link before noticing the cat3Risky links blocked until checked; bigger cat
A “% scam” score was confusing2A verdict in words: “Likely a scam”
No way to go back in the conversation2“Go back” on every question
Unclear what to do at the end2A “What should I do?” step
Wanted to know why1A “Why?” explanation in simple words
Small text; cat hard to see in dark mode1Bigger text and stronger contrast

Prototype: High Fidelity

Working web app & key design choices

THE SHIFT

From info dump to one step at a time

Early versions put the score, the reasons and every option on one screen. Older adults learn best step by step, with someone they trust¹, and crowded screens add cognitive load².

So C@T now asks one question at a time.

DESIGN DECISIONS

  • A familiar email inbox, so there is nothing new to learn.
  • A minimal layout in calm colours.
  • The cat waits quietly at the top and speaks up only when something looks wrong.
  • Verdicts in words, never colour alone.

ACCESSIBILITY

  • A comfort bar: bigger text, read-aloud and high contrast.
  • Irish and Arabic, with right-to-left layout.
  • A clear label on every icon.
  • Large tap targets, following WCAG 2.2.

11 → 0

IMPACT Accessibility checks went from 11 problems to 0.

¹ Ghadamighalandari et al., 2026. ² Hu, Choe & Lazar, 2026.

Prototype: Design Process

From moodboard to onboarding screens

MOODBOARD

ONBOARDING: WIREFRAMES TO FIGMA

Six wireframe steps, one idea each: the verdict at the top, locked links, text size and a trusted contact.

IN FIGMA

The steps moved onto an eight-column grid: one question per screen, a step counter, a language switch, and Back and Next on every step.

Future Work & Limitations

Limitations

SYNTHETIC DATA & PERSONAS

Problem statements and personas are based on current research and synthetic personas only.

TARGET USER EVALUATION

Not tested with actual target elderly users; evaluated using student proxies taking user roles.

DEMO SCOPE

The current demo represents a horizontal slice of user interaction across features.

Feasibility Issues to Address

MALICIOUS CONTENT DETECTION

Automated identification of malicious content is currently not implemented and needs integration.

DEVICE PERFORMANCE

The application may experience performance constraints when running on older hardware devices.
